followUps: I weigh growth the most, meaning how much I will learn and how my scope can expand, because it compounds. Situation: I once chose between a higher-paying maintenance role and a smaller team owning a new service. Action: I scored growth at 40 percent, pay 25, manager 20, stability 15. Result: the new-service offer won by about 0.6 points even though it paid roughly 8 percent less, and within two years my scope and pay passed the other path.

I talk to the people, not only the hiring manager. I ask to meet two or three future teammates and ask each the same questions: how are decisions made, what happened in the last incident, how does feedback work, why did the last person leave. I also look for people who have been there over a year and have been promoted. If answers are vague or they contradict each other, I count that as a warning. I then write down what I heard and score it, rather than trusting my gut after a friendly chat.

A strike price is the fixed price per share you pay when you exercise an option, set on the grant date. Example: the strike is $2 and the shares are worth $10 when you exercise, so each share costs you $2 and has $8 of paper gain (before tax). If the shares are worth $1.50, the option is under water and exercising would lose money, so you simply do not exercise. For 10,000 options at a $2 strike, exercising costs $20,000 in cash. That is why I always ask what the strike is and how recent the company valuation behind it is.

It is the period after you leave a company during which you may still exercise your vested options; after it, they expire. Many startups give only 90 days, which can force a decision on a large cash bill (and tax) within three months. For example, 10,000 options at a $2 strike need $20,000 within 90 days of leaving. Some companies offer longer windows, such as several years. I ask about it before accepting, because a short window can make vested options effectively unusable if I do not have the cash.

I ask politely, with a reason, and offer a trade. I would say that I love the role but a flatter schedule fits my plan, for example 25/25/25/25 instead of 5/15/40/40, or a larger first-year share, or a refresher grant at month 12. Companies often cannot change the total, but they may change the shape, so I propose a package of equal value over four years. Keep it a request, not an ultimatum, and get the agreed change in the written offer. If they refuse, I price the schedule into my comparison instead.

Acceleration means some unvested shares vest early if a trigger happens. Single trigger vests on the event itself (for example a company sale); double trigger needs two events, such as a sale and then a layoff. Layoff protection is uncommon for ordinary employees, but severance with a few months of extra vesting can be asked for, mostly at senior levels. I would ask whether any exists, and not rely on it. Example: if 20 percent of my grant would vest in the next quarter, acceleration would be worth that whole chunk.

I ask whether the band is fixed for the base only, and then move the conversation to other levers that are usually flexible. Those are sign-on bonus, equity amount, level, a start date, a six-month review with a raise, remote days or learning budget. Example: base is capped at 150k, so I ask for a 25k sign-on and a larger equity grant to close a 30k gap. Then I thank them and let them check. I am honest that the total matters to me. If every lever is fixed, I decide on growth and fit.

I build it from data, not from my feelings. I check several salary sources for the role, level, city and company size, and talk to peers. Suppose the market range is 140k to 170k and I am strong for the level: I would target near the top, say 165k, and ask for it with a short reason. I choose a number slightly above my real goal to leave room for a counter, and I also know my walk-away minimum of 150k before the call. I never name a number I could not justify.

I would stay polite and explain that I am not hiding anything; I would rather match on the role's level and range. I might say: I am happy to share my target range of 150k to 170k, which reflects this role. If the recruiter still insists and says they cannot continue, I treat it as a process question, not a reason to panic. I can decide whether to share a number once, calmly, or to step out. A company that refuses any discussion without my old salary tells me how they will treat pay later.

Yes, sometimes, when it helps me and I choose it. For example, my current pay is well above the range, or I am going to a place that asks for it to check the match, and I know the law allows it. I can share total compensation rather than only base, and say it with context. I never inflate it, because offers can be verified and a lie ends the relationship. If my current pay is low, I do not volunteer it. The rule is to decide on purpose before the call.

I decide with my criteria, not with fear. Situation: an offer expired in 48 hours and the other process had two weeks left. Action: I asked for three days, was refused, then compared the offer to my must-haves and my fallback, my current job. Result: the offer lacked the team I wanted, so I declined politely and kept in touch. If the offer clearly passes my bar, I accept. A refused extension is information about the culture, not a reason to say yes to a poor fit.

I write a short, honest email: I have an offer with a deadline of Friday, your company is my strong interest, and I would like to know if the process can move faster. I give a real date and no pressure or invented detail, and I do not share the other company's name or pay unless I choose to. Companies often compress a schedule, for example from three weeks to one week, when asked early and clearly. If they cannot, I accept that and decide with the information I have.

I would ask for a direct, written answer: what changed, and what will be different in six months. Situation: my manager offered a 12 percent raise after I resigned. Action: I asked why it had not come in the last review and checked my real issue, which was the scope, not pay. Result: the answer was budget timing and no change in scope, so I kept my resignation. A late offer often shows that the raise comes only under threat, and that tells me how future requests would go.

I tell them early and respectfully, by phone or a short email, with a clear reason that is true and not blaming. For example: I received a counter-offer, I thought carefully, and I am staying because the scope I asked for was put in writing. If I had accepted their offer, I should say so quickly and thank them for the time, since recruiters remember how people behave. I do not leak details about my current company. A good, kind message keeps the door open for later, and the industry is smaller than it looks.

I would go back if the weekly work stopped giving me energy, for example if I spend most days in meetings and approvals and feel my technical skills fading. I would set that test beforehand: after six months I rate my days on energy and on results for the team, and I ask my own manager and two reports for feedback. If the answer is no, I move back through the written way back, which I agreed at the start. Going back is a normal career choice, not a failure, and many strong leaders do it.

The main change is that your output becomes other people's output. As an IC you are judged on code and design; as a manager you are judged on how well the team delivers, grows and stays. New skills include one-on-ones, giving hard feedback, hiring, planning and clear writing, and conflict handling. Example: instead of fixing a bug myself in 2 hours, I might spend 2 hours coaching someone so they fix the next three alone. Technical depth still matters, but you use it by asking good questions.

I would be honest that I may not have it yet, and ask what is missing to reach the level. Then I ask for a written plan: two or three concrete goals, such as leading one cross-team project and mentoring a junior, with a review in six months. Meanwhile I accept the lower level only if the pay and growth are still good, and I do not claim work I did not do. Example: if I lead a project that saves 20 percent of build time, that is evidence for next time. Evidence beats arguments.

Level names do not match across companies: a senior at one place can be mid-level at another. So I compare by scope and expectations, not title. I ask about years of experience, size of problems owned, and who they report to or influence, and I use public leveling data carefully. Example: Company A senior might own one feature, while Company B senior might own a system with two teams depending on it. I match levels by that, and pay bands then make sense to compare.

One example: I asked an assistant for a database query and it used a column that does not exist; it sounded confident, and the code looked fine. I ran it against a test table, saw the error, and checked the schema docs. I fixed it and added a rule to always run generated code on sample data. Outcome: no bad change shipped. The lesson is that AI output is a draft to verify, and strong fundamentals let me spot a wrong answer quickly.

I will stop hand-typing repetitive work: boilerplate, simple tests, first drafts of docs, and quick scripts to reshape data. For example, writing 20 similar unit test cases by hand takes about 40 minutes; with AI and a review it takes about 10. I will not stop doing the thinking: choosing the design, reading the code carefully, and checking edge cases. I review every generated change as if a new teammate wrote it. The time saved goes toward design, reliability and talking to users.

I protect my energy by keeping the plan small and regular rather than heroic. I fix three hours a week in a calendar slot, take one week off each quarter, and drop topics that no longer matter. For example, when I tried five hours daily for a month, I got tired and my work suffered, so I returned to a lighter rhythm and kept the habit for a year. I also mix reading with building something small. Rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.

I measure outputs, not hours. Each quarter I check three things: what I built or shared (a demo, a note, a talk), what I can now do without help, and feedback from my manager or mentor against the ladder. A simple target could be: finish two small projects, write four short notes, and move one skill from needs help to independent. Then I update my brag document. If nothing visible changed after three months, I change the method.

I assume 0 percent growth as the base case, so the comparison relies on the real terms, and I add a cautious case of minus 20 percent and an optimistic case of 10 percent a year. Example: a 200k grant over four years is 50k a year at 0 percent; at minus 20 percent the year 4 vest is worth about 33k less than at 0 percent. If one offer still wins in all three cases, the choice is robust. I do not trust a fast growth story.

I treat it as a lottery ticket with a heavy discount, not as cash. I ask for the latest valuation, number of shares outstanding, preferences and strike price, to estimate the percentage I own. A common rule is to value it at 0 to 30 percent of the paper number, depending on the stage. Example: shares worth 100k on paper count as 20k in my comparison. I base my decision on salary and growth, and treat equity as upside. Liquidity is not guaranteed.

I keep my word, so I would honor the accepted offer unless there is a serious reason. Backing out after accepting damages trust and my reputation, and recruiters talk. If something truly changes, such as a much better role that is a clear fit, I would speak to the first company right away, honestly and respectfully, rather than sending a short message on the start date. The right moment to compare is before I say yes. So I always ask for the timeline first and tell other companies I am deciding.

I share as much as is needed and no more: the timeline, and generally what matters to me, such as level or total compensation range. I do not share names or exact numbers unless I choose to, because they may be confidential and it can read as pressure. Example: I might say another offer is higher on base but I prefer your team; can the sign-on be 20k? That is true, specific and respectful. I never invent or inflate an offer, since I may be asked to prove it.
